indications: Symptomatic gallstone disease: biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, gallstone pancreatitis after recovery, and choledocholithiasis after duct clearance.
Acute calculous cholecystitis: early cholecystectomy on the index admission has better outcomes than delayed surgery.
Gallbladder polyps meeting size or growth criteria, and porcelain gallbladder.
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy or an unfit patient in whom percutaneous cholecystostomy is the better source control.
Suspected gallbladder carcinoma, which needs an oncological plan rather than a routine cholecystectomy.
Inability to tolerate pneumoperitoneum. This favours an open approach rather than no operation.
preparation: Ultrasound to confirm stones, wall thickening and duct diameter; liver function tests to interrogate the duct.
Clear the duct first if choledocholithiasis is confirmed, or plan an intra-operative approach to it.
Antibiotic prophylaxis; therapeutic antibiotics if this is an inflamed gallbladder.
Consent must include conversion to open, bile duct injury, bile leak, retained stones, and injury to bowel or vessels.
positioning: Supine, reverse Trendelenburg with left tilt so the colon and duodenum fall away from the porta.
Arms out or tucked according to whether the American or French position is used.
Monitor sited so the surgeon looks along the axis of dissection.
equipment: Four ports typically: 10 mm umbilical camera, 10 mm epigastric, two 5 mm right subcostal.
30-degree scope, hook diathermy, Maryland dissector, clip applier, retrieval bag.
Facility for intra-operative cholangiography or laparoscopic ultrasound.
An open set immediately available in theatre, not in the store.
anatomy: Calot triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior border of the liver. The cystic artery usually lies within it.
Anatomical variation is the rule, not the exception: an accessory or aberrant right hepatic duct, a short cystic duct, and a right hepatic artery running close to the gallbladder are all common.
Rouviere sulcus marks the plane of the right portal pedicle and is a reliable external landmark: dissection stays anterior to it.
The cystic plate lies between the gallbladder and the liver; staying on it avoids both liver bleeding and injury to structures behind.
criticalSafety: Achieve the Critical View of Safety before dividing anything: the hepatocystic triangle cleared of fat and fibrous tissue, the lower third of the gallbladder separated from the cystic plate, and exactly two structures seen entering the gallbladder.
The Critical View is a view, not a manoeuvre. If it cannot be obtained, do not proceed to clip.
Bail out rather than persist: subtotal cholecystectomy, conversion, or cholecystostomy and come back. A bail-out is a good outcome; a bile duct injury is not.
structuresAtRisk: Common bile duct and common hepatic duct
Right hepatic artery and an aberrant right hepatic duct
Duodenum and hepatic flexure of the colon
Liver bed, causing troublesome venous bleeding
commonErrors: The classical injury pattern: the common bile duct mistaken for the cystic duct because traction was applied upwards rather than laterally.
Dissecting high on the gallbladder wall in the wrong plane and entering the liver, or too low and approaching the porta.
Persisting laparoscopically for another twenty minutes because conversion feels like failure.
Using energy near the common bile duct, causing a delayed thermal stricture that presents weeks later.
complications: Bile duct injury, the complication that defines this operation. Recognised intra-operatively it is retrievable; recognised late it is life-changing.
Bile leak from the cystic duct stump or a duct of Luschka.
Bleeding from the cystic artery or the liver bed.
Port-site hernia, wound infection, and dropped stones causing a late intra-abdominal abscess.
postop: Same-day or next-day discharge for an uncomplicated elective case.
Persistent pain, tachycardia, or a rising bilirubin after cholecystectomy is a bile leak or a duct injury until imaging says otherwise. Do not attribute it to wind.
Discuss any suspected duct injury with a hepatobiliary unit immediately. Do not attempt a repair without that expertise.
Follow up the histology: an unexpected gallbladder carcinoma changes the whole plan.

steps.emphasis: Reverse Trendelenburg with left tilt does more for exposure at the porta than any retractor.
Always use a bag. A perforated gallbladder that spills stones into the abdomen produces an abscess months later.

step.chole.retraction.title: Retraction: fundus up, infundibulum lateral
step.chole.retraction.why: The single commonest cause of bile duct injury is retraction that aligns the cystic duct with the common bile duct, so the two look like one tube.
how: Retract the fundus cephalad over the liver edge.
Retract the infundibulum LATERALLY and inferiorly, never upwards. This opens the hepatocystic triangle and separates the two ducts.
Re-establish this retraction every time it is lost. Almost every difficult moment in this operation is a retraction problem.
pitfalls: Cephalad traction on the infundibulum, which tents the common bile duct into the field.

step.chole.cvs.title: The Critical View of Safety
step.chole.cvs.why: This is the step the whole operation exists around. It is a positive confirmation of anatomy, and it is the only one that reliably prevents the classical bile duct injury.
how: Clear the hepatocystic triangle of all fat and fibrous tissue. It does not require exposure of the common bile duct.
Separate the lower third of the gallbladder from the cystic plate.
Confirm that exactly two structures, and only two, are seen entering the gallbladder.
Pause, state the view aloud to the team, and document it. If you cannot achieve it, take a bail-out option.
pitfalls: Declaring the view when only the anterior aspect has been cleared.
Achieving a 'nearly' critical view and proceeding anyway.

step.chole.divide.title: Clipping and dividing the cystic duct and artery
step.chole.divide.why: Once a structure is divided, an error becomes an injury. Everything before this step is reversible; this step is not.
how: Only after the Critical View: place clips on the cystic artery and duct, leaving an adequate stump on the retained side.
Divide between clips under direct vision, with the tips of the clip applier seen on both sides.
Consider intra-operative cholangiography where anatomy is uncertain or the duct may contain stones.
A cystic duct too wide or too inflamed for a clip needs a loop or a suture, not a bigger clip.
pitfalls: Clipping with the far tip out of view.
Dividing before the view, intending to 'see better afterwards'.

step.chole.plate.title: Separating the gallbladder from the cystic plate
step.chole.plate.why: The plane between the gallbladder and the cystic plate is nearly bloodless. Straying above it bleeds from the liver; straying below it perforates the gallbladder.
how: Work in the areolar plane with gentle counter-traction, hook diathermy in short controlled bursts.
Before detaching the fundus, inspect the gallbladder bed and the clips one final time while the gallbladder is still held.
Deal with a perforation promptly: retrieve spilled stones and irrigate.
structuresAtRisk: Ducts of Luschka in the cystic plate
pitfalls: Detaching the fundus before inspecting the bed, losing the retraction that exposes it.
